title: Episode 1: Gokul Rajaram on Product Strategy
speaker: Gokul Rajaram
content:
Lenny: Welcome Gokul. You've been at Google, Facebook, Square, DoorDash. What's the common thread in your product philosophy?

Gokul: The common thread is really about understanding the user problem deeply before building solutions. At each company, I've seen teams jump to solutions without truly understanding the 'why'. The best products come from obsessing over the problem space.

Lenny: Can you give a specific example from DoorDash?

Gokul: At DoorDash, the initial problem wasn't 'food delivery' - it was 'how do we help local restaurants survive and grow?' That reframing changed everything. We built tools for restaurant onboarding, logistics optimization, and customer acquisition. The product wasn't the app - it was the platform enabling restaurants.

Lenny: How do you define product-market fit?

Gokul: PMF is when users are pulling the product out of your hands. Quantitatively, it's 40%+ very disappointed users if the product disappeared (Sean Ellis test). Qualitatively, it's when you stop pushing and start scaling. At DoorDash, we knew we had PMF when restaurants started calling us begging to join, not the other way around.

Lenny: What about growth strategies?

Gokul: Growth isn't a tactic - it's a system. You need: 1) A core product that delivers value, 2) A distribution channel that scales, 3) A monetization model that sustains. Most startups fail at #1 or #2. At Square, the card reader was the wedge, but the POS system created the moat.

Lenny: How do you prioritize features?

Gokul: I use the RICE framework but modified: Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort. But the key is Confidence - how sure are you about Impact? At Facebook, we'd run small experiments to increase confidence before big bets. Data beats opinions.

Lenny: Any advice for early-stage PMs?

Gokul: Talk to users every week. Not surveys - real conversations. The best PMs I know spend 50%+ of their time with users. Also, learn to write clearly. Writing is thinking. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough.
